tldr: DiffGIPC is a GPU-accelerated differentiable simulator that enables fast, strictly penetration-free differentiation of complex collision and friction between deformable and nearly rigid bodies, achieving up to 4133x speedups over DiffIPC.
hero_caption: Placement optimization for stacking seven stones into a tall tower. While keeping the stone geometries fixed, gradients from contact and friction are used to adjust initial horizontal placements, automatically generating a stable, self-standing stack that does not collapse.
overview:
When robots grasp flexible objects or manipulate garments, they need to solve inverse problems that optimize design or control parameters using gradients, accurately predicting collisions and friction between objects. However, existing differentiable simulators either rely on penalty methods that allow penetration, or, when using Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) to strictly prevent penetration, suffer from extreme computational cost because every part is modeled with fine finite-element method (FEM) meshes.

To address this, the authors propose a mixed-coordinate framework that pairs full-space FEM where deformation is needed with affine bodies (ABD) that require only 12 degrees of freedom (DoFs) per object for nearly rigid components. Furthermore, they formulate a trajectory adjoint method that correctly preserves the history-dependent nature of contact and friction backward in time, and build an end-to-end GPU pipeline using conditional CUDA Graphs to execute linear solver iterations and convergence checks entirely on the GPU.

In validation experiments on the same FEM benchmarks used by the CPU-based DiffIPC, DiffGIPC achieved 12.3x to 34.1x speedups across the entire backward computation. Furthermore, when substituting nearly rigid components with affine bodies on high-resolution models, it achieved an overwhelming speedup of up to 4133.3x, demonstrating fast optimization across diverse tasks such as garment-hanger shape design and dynamic cup catching with a robotic arm.
contributions: Proposed a differentiable IPC framework supporting contact, friction, and joint constraints within a mixed-coordinate system that combines deformable FEM with affine bodies having only 12 DoFs per object.

Derived gradient computations for affine bodies by evaluating mass and inertia derivatives directly from surface mesh integrals, enabling efficient inverse optimization of rest shapes, initial states, and articulated control inputs.
Constructed an all-GPU-parallel pipeline for solving the adjoint system, eliminating CPU-GPU synchronization overhead in the iterative solver (PCG) using conditional CUDA Graphs.
Provided a seamless PyTorch interface and achieved forward and backward speedups of up to over 4133x compared to DiffIPC.

sections.heading: Can We Solve Contact-Rich Inverse Problems Without Penetration at Ultra-High Speed?
sections.summary: Optimizing objects through contact and friction demands accurate gradients that track force transmission. However, existing differentiable simulations force a choice between tolerating penetration and suffering enormous computational costs. This paper presents DiffGIPC, which handles deformable and rigid-like bodies in mixed coordinates and differentiates them fully in parallel on the GPU.
sections.details:
Many robotics tasks require optimizing the behavior of one object by altering the parameters of another, such as grasping soft items or hanging garments. In these contact-rich inverse problems, gradient information that accurately captures forces transmitted through collision and friction is essential.

Existing differentiable simulators have suffered from two major weaknesses. First, methods emphasizing computational speed rely on penalty formulations or velocity-level constraints (like DiffPD or DiffPhD), which permit penetration and positional drift during sustained contact. Second, DiffIPC completely prevents penetration using geometric barrier functions and continuous collision detection (CCD), but CPU-based computation is extremely slow because even rigid parts retain fine FEM vertex degrees of freedom.

This paper focuses on combining GPU parallelism with a mixed-coordinate formulation that cuts redundant motion representations. While retaining full-space FEM for regions needing local deformation, affine bodies (ABD) with only 12 DoFs per object are assigned to components that behave as nearly rigid. This drastically reduces the size of equations solved during backward passes while fully differentiating interactions through contact and joints.

sections.heading: Prior Work: The Trade-Off Between Contact Accuracy and Computational Efficiency
sections.summary: Differentiable physics simulation has progressed in both speed and contact accuracy, but no prior method achieved both strict non-penetration and low computational cost at a high level. This work overcomes this challenge by pairing IPC's exact contact protection with affine DoF reduction and dedicated GPU solvers.
sections.details:
### The Evolution of Differentiable Contact Simulation
Gradient-based system identification and control have been actively researched. Methods using Projective Dynamics (PD), such as DiffPD and DiffCloth, gained speed by reusing pre-factored matrices, but cannot fully prevent penetration due to penalty-based contact. In contrast, Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains a feasible region using barrier energies, mathematically preventing mesh intersections. DiffIPC extended this to be differentiable, but because it modeled even rigid parts using full-space FEM, iterative inverse solves remained extremely heavy.

### Compact Motion Coordinates
Reducing the coordinate space is effective for cutting the computational burden of nearly rigid parts. While approaches like Rigid IPC handle exact rigid rotation, Affine Body Dynamics (ABD) introduces a mild stiffness energy to represent motion using 12 DoFs across translation and affine transformation. Because surface vertices of an ABD move linearly with respect to these DoFs, collision trajectories are easy to handle and mass matrix structures remain simple.

### Accelerating Trajectory Adjoints on GPU
Methods like DiffPhD solve quickly on the GPU by reusing fixed matrix factorizations. In IPC, however, the Hessian changes every frame according to deformation and contact states, preventing matrix reuse. Consequently, running iterative preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) methods efficiently on the GPU becomes critically important.

sections.heading: A One-Step Differentiable Framework Solved in Mixed Coordinates
sections.summary: The 3 DoFs of deformable vertices and the 12 DoFs of affine bodies are unified into a single system, formulated as an incremental potential minimization problem. By mapping contact and friction energies from surface vertices into mixed coordinates, one-step adjoint equations are derived while preserving inter-object couplings.
sections.details:
### Simulation Degrees of Freedom and Contact Points
A free FEM vertex $i$ possesses a 3D position vector $\mathbf{x}_{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Meanwhile, affine body $b$ is represented by 12 degrees of freedom $\mathbf{q}_{t,b}$, arranging translation $\mathbf{p}_{t,b} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and the rows of affine transformation matrix $\mathbf{A}_{t,b} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$. Surface vertex positions are determined by a simple linear relation $\mathbf{x}_{t,i} = \mathbf{p}_{t,b} + \mathbf{A}_{t,b} \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i$ (where $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i$ is the rest position), with its Jacobian defined as $\mathbf{J}_i$. Total simulation DoFs are $n = 12N_{\mathrm{A}} + 3N_{\mathrm{F}}$, meaning refining an affine body's mesh never increases the number of motion DoFs.

### Incremental Potential and Stationarity Conditions
At each time step $t$, the simulation minimizes an incremental potential, which sums inertial terms with elastic, collision, friction, and joint energies. At convergence, the stationarity condition holds: energy gradient $\mathbf{g}_t(\mathbf{y}_t, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{y}_t$ denotes simulation DoFs and $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ denotes physical parameters targeted for optimization.

### Deriving Parameter Gradients via the Adjoint Method
Differentiating the stationarity condition yields $\mathbf{H}_t \mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_t + \mathbf{G}_t \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{H}_t$ is the energy Hessian and $\mathbf{G}_t$ is the partial derivative with respect to parameters. Explicitly computing $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}_t/\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}$ to obtain the gradient of a scalar loss $L$ scales poorly with parameter count. Thus, the adjoint method is used: solving the adjoint system $\mathbf{H}_t \boldsymbol{\lambda} = \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L$ for adjoint vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$, and computing the loss gradient as $-\mathbf{G}_t^{\mathsf{T}} \boldsymbol{\lambda}$.

### Cross-Representation Mapping for Contact and Friction Derivatives
Contact barrier and friction energies are evaluated at surface vertex positions in 3D world space. These are assembled into the mixed-coordinate Hessian via mapping matrix $\mathbf{K}_{t,c}$. Contact between affine bodies forms a $12\times 12$ block, while contact between an affine body and an FEM vertex forms a $12\times 3$ block, firmly preserving interactions in the off-diagonal entries of the Hessian.

sections.heading: Rewinding Time: A Trajectory Adjoint Accounting for History Dependencies
sections.summary: To find loss gradients across an entire trajectory, an algorithm is derived that marches backward from the final frame to the initial frame, solving one coupled adjoint system per frame. Velocity predictions from inertia and dependencies on past contact states from friction are both accurately backpropagated.
sections.details:
### Trajectory-Wide Equations and Causality
The stationarity condition at frame $t$ depends not only on current DoFs $\mathbf{y}_t$, but also on past states (under BDF1 time integration, $t-1$ and $t-2$). Arranging the equations across the entire trajectory forms a block lower triangular matrix due to temporal causality. In the adjoint method, taking the transpose produces a block upper triangular matrix, enabling a backward solve from final frame $T$ down to $t=1$ via back-substitution.

### One Adjoint Solve Per Frame
In the backward time loop, Hessian $\mathbf{H}_t$ is assembled once from stored converged states at each frame $t$, solving the linear system $\mathbf{H}_t \boldsymbol{\lambda}_t = \mathbf{b}_t$ for that frame's right-hand side $\mathbf{b}_t$. Using the resulting adjoint vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$, the algorithm accumulates contributions $\Delta\mathbf{b}_s^{(t)}$ to past right-hand sides $\mathbf{b}_s$ upon which the frame depended, along with gradient contributions $\Delta\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(t)}$ for optimization parameters.

### Past-Frame Dependencies of Inertia and Friction
Derivatives of inertial terms propagate to past states through mass matrix $\mathbf{M}$. Additionally, because the IPC friction model determines contact tangent bases and normal forces from the previous frame's relative positions, friction energy gradients depend on past positions $\mathbf{y}_{t-1}$. This framework maps these dependency derivatives into mixed coordinates and adds them into past-frame right-hand sides, achieving accurate gradient propagation through sliding friction.

sections.heading: Shape, Initial States, and Articulated Control: Differentiating Affine Body Parameters Freely
sections.summary: The method enables rich parameter exploration while preserving the lightweight 12-DoF nature of affine bodies. Mass and inertia shape derivatives are obtained directly from surface integrals over closed meshes, rigorously formulating gradients for rest shapes, initial states, and articulated control inputs.
sections.details:
### Mass and Inertia Derivatives from Surface Meshes
The mass matrix $\mathbf{M}_b$ of an affine body is determined by three volume integrals: total mass, first mass moment, and second mass moment. Using the divergence theorem, this approach evaluates these volume integrals directly from vertex coordinates of oriented surface triangles. This yields exact implicit mass matrix derivatives $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{M}_b$ with respect to surface vertex positions without generating internal tetrahedral meshes.

### Rest-Shape Gradients and Contact/Friction Effects
Modifying an affine body's rest shape alters not only inertia, but also world-space contact locations and mapping matrix $\mathbf{K}_{t,c}$. For contact barrier energy, gradients account for both changes in contact forces from moving surface vertices and changes in lever arms transmitting forces to affine DoFs. For friction, the shift in identical material point positions between previous and current frames is rigorously incorporated.

### Derivatives for Initial States and Articulated Parameters
Initial positions $\mathbf{q}_0$ and velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_0$ influence equations through predictors in the first and second frames. Their derivatives are easily accumulated via products with adjoint vectors. For robotic joints (revolute and prismatic), tracking potentials toward target angles and applied torques are introduced, enabling gradients with respect to these control inputs to be computed consistently through the same adjoint system.

sections.heading: No Idling GPUs: An All-GPU Pipeline Powered by CUDA Graphs
sections.summary: As affine bodies shrink linear systems, CPU kernel-launch overheads become prominent. By using conditional CUDA Graphs to encapsulate PCG iterations and convergence checks within the GPU, a flexible pipeline was built that connects seamlessly with PyTorch.
sections.details:
### Accelerating PCG with Conditional CUDA Graphs
When mixed coordinates shrink the linear system size, raw numerical computation decreases, but CPU-side iteration loops and convergence checks (kernel launch and synchronization latencies) begin to dominate runtime. To resolve this, conditional CUDA Graphs package PCG iteration steps and residual checks together on the GPU. The CPU launches the graph once, and the GPU loops autonomously until convergence, completely eliminating unnecessary synchronization.

### GPU-Parallel Gradient Accumulation
After computing adjoint vector $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$, parameter gradients are evaluated in parallel by independent GPU threads per FEM element, contact pair, joint, and affine surface triangle, avoiding large global $\mathbf{G}_t$ matrices in memory. Contributions to shared parameters are accumulated via atomic additions, ensuring high memory efficiency and scalability.

### Reusable Interface with PyTorch
User-defined maps from design variables to physical parameters, as well as loss function maps from simulation states to metrics, are handled by PyTorch's automatic differentiation. DiffGIPC exclusively handles differentiation of the physics simulation. This enables intuitive application across shape design, system identification, and robotic control without modifying simulator core routines.

captions.F5: PCG solver execution control flow. (a) Computation steps within a single iteration, (b) conventional method with CPU-GPU synchronization every iteration, and (c) the proposed approach using conditional CUDA Graphs to run autonomously through convergence checks inside the GPU, zeroing out synchronization overhead.

sections.heading: Performance Evaluation: Dramatic Speedups and Diverse Practical Applications
sections.summary: Effectiveness was verified through DiffIPC comparisons, resolution scaling with affine bodies, and diverse robotics and design tasks. Combining GPU execution with affine representations achieved speedups up to 4133x alongside highly accurate gradient evaluations.
sections.details:
### Benchmark Comparisons with DiffIPC
Performance was compared on the same low-resolution FEM benchmarks as DiffIPC (bunny drop, tentacle tracking, support structure design, material property identification, and slider friction identification). Even when both used full-space FEM, DiffGIPC was 12.3x to 34.1x faster on backward passes alone, and 10.6x to 60.9x faster in combined forward and backward computation.

### Motion Representations and Resolution Scaling
In a bunny collision task, mesh resolution was scaled from 933 to 28,435 vertices. At the highest resolution, treating rigid-like bunnies as affine bodies (ABD) reduced backward linear solve time from 2.3 seconds to 0.0044 seconds compared to full-space FEM—about a 520x speedup. Compared to the CPU-based DiffIPC FEM baseline, overall forward-backward speedup reached 4133.3x.

### Design, Placement, and Robot Control Tasks
- **Clothes Hanger Shape Design**: Optimized shoulder profiles to prevent friction-mediated garment slippage.
- **Seven-Stone Stacking**: Optimized initial horizontal positions to generate a stable, self-standing stone tower while maintaining complex contact geometries.
- **Dynamic Robot Arm Catching**: Optimized 700 joint targets for an xArm gripper holding a plate to catch a flying cup smoothly, absorbing impact without slipping.
- **Dual-Arm Towel Grasping**: Inverted appropriate vertical pinching depth from target contact forces to pinch and lift a towel.

### Gradient Verification and CUDA Graph Impact
Analytic gradients showed extremely small relative errors compared to central finite differences. Enabling CUDA Graphs provided an additional 1.3x to 1.8x speedup in PCG alone, and 1.2x to 1.5x speedup across complete forward-backward passes.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Toward Truly Contact-Rich Optimization
sections.summary: DiffGIPC drastically accelerates penetration-free differentiable contact simulation by pairing mixed-coordinate DoF reduction with a fully GPU-parallel pipeline. Future challenges include vanishing gradients when initial trajectories lack contact, as well as differentiating through remeshing.
sections.details:
DiffGIPC is a breakthrough framework that solves contact-rich inverse problems in practical computation times by combining mixed coordinates of deformable and affine bodies with GPU optimizations, all while maintaining IPC's robust guarantee against penetration.

Several challenges remain. First, because IPC barrier energies are local repulsive forces, contact gradients vanish when objects do not contact in initial trajectories, leaving optimization without a search direction; introducing long-range contact potentials is an attractive direction. Second, remeshing decisions made during optimization are not differentiated, leaving topology-changing problems as another avenue for future work.

takeaways: Substituting nearly rigid parts with 12-DoF affine bodies (ABD) dramatically compresses adjoint system size without lowering contact mesh resolution.
Encapsulating PCG iterations and convergence checks on the GPU via conditional CUDA Graphs eliminates kernel launch overheads that bottleneck small linear systems.
Shape derivatives of mass matrices can be evaluated directly from surface mesh integrals, allowing 3D geometric design of affine bodies without internal volumetric meshes.
Correctly backpropagating history dependencies in contact and friction enables gradient-based optimization for challenging robotics tasks like garment manipulation and dynamic catching.
limitations: Because localized barrier functions are used, contact gradients vanish when objects start too far apart in initial trajectories, causing optimization that needs to create new contacts to stall.
When remeshing is performed between optimization iterations, the geometric changes introduced by remeshing itself are not treated differentiably.
Because affine bodies only represent uniform stretch and shear, they cannot model high-stiffness parts that undergo localized bending or large deformations.
